description.summary: window decoration split between client and compositor

protocol.description:
Trinix draws window decorations in the client, and handles the interaction with them in the compositor.
That split is the whole reason this protocol exists. Client-side decorations let an application look like itself: the toolkit knows its own fonts, its own metrics, and what belongs in a title bar. What the toolkit does *not* know is where the window is on screen, what is behind it, or what the pointer was doing before it arrived — so shadows, window dragging, resize edges and the hover behaviour of the close/minimise/zoom controls are all handled here, by the compositor, which knows all three.
A client using this protocol therefore draws its own title bar and its own control glyphs, and tells the compositor where it put them. The compositor hit-tests them, reports hover and activation back, and renders the shadow underneath. Neither side duplicates the other's work.
Warning! This protocol is Trinix's own and is not stable. It is versioned, and a bump means clients must be rebuilt.

interface.name: trinix_shell_v1
interface.description: A global whose only job is to hand out trinix_shell_surface_v1 objects for xdg toplevels.

request.name: destroy
request.description: Destroying this object does not affect surfaces created from it.

request.name: get_shell_surface
request.description: Gives the toplevel Trinix's decoration behaviour. It is a protocol error to request a second shell surface for the same toplevel.

event.name: capabilities

description.summary: what this compositor will actually do

event.description: Sent once, immediately after binding. A client must not assume any capability it was not told about: a compositor running without a GPU may decline to blur, and one running on a memory-constrained device may decline to shadow, and in both cases the client's own decorations are still correct.

entry.name: shadow
entry.summary: the compositor can draw drop shadows

entry.name: rounded_corners
entry.summary: the compositor can round and clip corners

entry.name: blur
entry.summary: the compositor can blur what is behind a surface

entry.name: already_extended
entry.summary: the toplevel already has a shell surface

entry.name: invalid_control
entry.summary: control zone outside the window geometry

interface.name: trinix_shell_surface_v1
interface.description:
Everything here is double-buffered against the *xdg surface's* configure cycle: a request takes effect on the next wl_surface.commit, so that a window which resizes and moves its close button does both in the same frame. There is no separate commit request for that reason.
Coordinates are surface-local, in the same space as xdg_surface.set_window_geometry — which is to say they exclude whatever invisible margin the client reserves for its own shadows, if any.

request.name: destroy
request.description: The window keeps its xdg_toplevel and stays mapped; it simply loses shadows and control hit-testing.

request.name: set_shadow
request.description: The shadow is drawn outside the window geometry, by the compositor, and is not part of any buffer the client allocates. Ignored if the compositor did not advertise the shadow capability.

request.name: set_corner_radius
request.description: In surface-local pixels; zero means square. The compositor clips the surface to the rounded rectangle, so the client need not punch its own corners out and need not care what is behind them.

request.name: set_drag_region
request.description:
Typically the title bar, minus the controls. A press inside this region that turns into a drag moves the window, and the client never sees the motion — which is what makes dragging smooth on a window whose main thread is busy.
A null region means the whole window, which is right for a panel and wrong for almost anything else.

request.name: set_resize_inset

description.summary: how far in from the edges a resize grab starts

request.description: A window whose resize edges are exactly its geometry edges is a window nobody can resize on a high-DPI display. The inset extends the grab area inwards; the compositor still consumes those events rather than delivering them to the client.

request.name: set_control

description.summary: declare a window control's hit zone

request.description:
The client draws the control; the compositor decides what pointing at it means. Sending the same control twice replaces the previous zone.
This is the part that makes the traffic lights behave: because the compositor owns the hit-testing, hovering any one control can light all three, and it can do so without waking the application at all.

event.name: control_activated
event.description: The compositor does not act on this itself. Closing a window is the application's decision — it may have unsaved work to ask about — so this is a request to the client, exactly as xdg_toplevel.close is.

event.name: control_hover

description.summary: the pointer entered or left the control group

event.description: Sent for the group rather than the individual control, because that is the behaviour being described: the glyphs appear when the pointer is anywhere over them. `control` names which one is under the pointer, or is unused when state is `left`.

event.name: shadow_applied

description.summary: the shadow the compositor actually drew

event.description: The margins the shadow occupies outside the window geometry, so a client that cares about its total footprint — for a screenshot, or to avoid placing a popup under its own shadow — can find out. All zero when there is no shadow.

entry.name: minimise
entry.summary: hide the window to the dock

entry.name: docked
entry.summary: a tight shadow, for panels and menus

entry.name: window
entry.summary: the shadow an ordinary window casts

entry.name: floating
entry.summary: a deeper shadow, for dialogs and popovers

entry.name: left
entry.summary: the pointer is no longer over any control

entry.name: entered
entry.summary: the pointer is over the named control

entry.name: pressed
entry.summary: the named control is being held down
